statement.p: Calculate the circulation, \int_C\vec F\cdot d\vec r, in two ways, directly and using Stokes' Theorem. The vector field \vec F = 2 y\vec i - 2 x\vec j and C is the boundary of S, the part of the surface z = 16 -x^2-y^2 above the xy-plane, oriented upward.
Note that C is a circle in the xy-plane. Find a \vec r(t) that parameterizes this curve.

p.em: (Note that answers must be provided for all three of these answer blanks to be able to determine correctness of the parameterization.)

statement.p: With this parameterization, the circulation integral is
\int_C\vec F\cdot d\vec r = \int_a^b dt, where a and b are the endpoints you gave above.

Using Stokes' Theorem, we equate \int_C\vec F\cdot d\vec r = \int_S\mbox{curl }\vec F\cdot d\vec A. Find \mbox{curl }\vec F = .
Noting that the surface is given by z = 16 - x^2 - y^2, find
With R giving the region in the xy-plane enclosed by the surface, this gives
Evaluate this integral to find the circulation:
\int_C \vec F\cdot d\vec r = \int_{S} \mbox{curl }\vec F\cdot d\vec A = .

static.solution:
C is the curve x^2+y^2=16, oriented counterclockwise, we calculate \int_C\vec F\cdot d\vec r directly using the parameterization x(t) = 4\cos t,\quad y(t)=4\sin t,\quad z(t)=0,\quad 0\le t\le 2\pi,\quad \hbox{ so } \vec r'(t)=-4\sin t\vec i+4\cos t\vec j. Thus, \int_C\vec F\cdot d\vec r = \int_0^{2\pi}(8\sin t\vec i-8\cos t\vec j)\cdot (-4\sin t\vec i+4\cos t\vec j)\, dt = -32\int_0^{2\pi}(\sin^2t+\cos^2t)\, dt = -32\cdot 2\pi = -64\pi.
Then, finding \mbox{curl }\vec F, we have \mbox{curl }\vec F=\left|\begin{array}{ccc} \vec i \amp \vec j \amp \vec k \\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x} \amp \frac{\partial}{\partial y} \amp \frac{\partial}{\partial z} \\ 2 y \ \ \amp -2 x \ \ \amp 0 \end{array}\right| =-4\vec k, Then if z = f(x,y), we know d\vec A = -f_x\vec i - f_y\vec j + \vec k, so d\vec A = 2x\vec i + 2y\vec j + \vec k, and \int_C\vec F\cdot d\vec r = \int_S\mbox{curl }\vec F\cdot d\vec A = \int_{R} -4\vec k\cdot(2x\vec i+2y\vec j+\vec k)\, dx\, dy = -4\int dx\,dy = -64\pi.
